articles.title: OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet Lets Agents Buy Things. One Bought a Potato
articles.excerpt: A guy on r/wallstreetbets put $200 into an AI shopping agent and let it buy his groceries. It ordered two of something. It picked the wrong variation of something else. And once, with no explanation,…
articles.body: A guy on r/wallstreetbets put $200 into an AI shopping agent and let it buy his groceries. It ordered two of something. It picked the wrong variation of something else. And once, with no explanation, it bought a single potato. i read that comment three times. Not because it was funny, though it is funny. Because one potato is the clearest summary of this whole product category i have seen so far. The agent did not fail in a dramatic way. It did not empty his account or buy a boat. It just quietly decided that one potato was the right amount of potato. That comment landed hours after OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet on November 13. The wallet lets agents in dots, ChatGPT Work, and Codex pay for things on your behalf. It was built with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa.

articles.title: Wiring the Keyright SDK into ASP.NET Core DI as a typed HttpClient with resilience
articles.excerpt: Most Keyright integrations start the same way: someone needs to validate a license against the self-hosted issuing service, so they write new HttpClient(), point it at the ServiceUrl, and ship it. It…
articles.body: Most Keyright integrations start the same way: someone needs to validate a license against the self-hosted issuing service, so they write new HttpClient() , point it at the ServiceUrl , and ship it. It works in development and on the demo. Then it goes to production and one of two things happens. Either the client is created per call — a fresh HttpClient inside the method that checks the license — and under real traffic the process runs out of sockets. Each disposed client leaves connections in TIME_WAIT , the ephemeral port range fills, and you start seeing SocketException: Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted .

articles.title: 10 PCB faults that pass DRC and still cause a respin
articles.excerpt: Your PCB passed DRC with zero errors. The Gerbers look clean in the viewer. So the board is ready for fab, right? Not quite. DRC checks the rules you gave the tool. It has no idea what the board is me…
articles.body: Your PCB passed DRC with zero errors. The Gerbers look clean in the viewer. So the board is ready for fab, right? Not quite. DRC checks the rules you gave the tool. It has no idea what the board is meant to do. In design reviews we keep finding the same small group of faults on boards that passed every automated check. Each one is cheap to fix on screen and expensive to fix after the boards come back. Here are ten of them, with the quick check that catches each one. 1. The right part with the wrong suffix A regulator, an LDO or a MOSFET can come in fixed and adjustable versions, or in two packages, under nearly the same part number. The schematic symbol is drawn for one variant and the BOM orders the other. DRC can't see it because the footprint is fine.

articles.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
articles.excerpt: Coding agents that work across successive tasks on an evolving repository face a memory problem: they must decide what to remember before they know what the next task will ask. Every memory segment co…
articles.body: Coding agents that work across successive tasks on an evolving repository face a memory problem: they must decide what to remember before they know what the next task will ask. Every memory segment costs tokens to write, tokens to retrieve, and context window space to store. The agent needs to predict which fragments will pay back those costs when the next task arrives. CoReMem (Coding-Repository Memory) treats memory selection as a cost-benefit problem. It measures the prospective value of each trajectory segment by running the next task twice: once with the segment included, once without. The difference in resolution rate and step count becomes the segment's measured value.

articles.title: Letting an AI assistant read SQL Server without letting it write
articles.excerpt: The problem The request sounds simple: let an AI assistant answer questions from a company's on-premises SQL Server. The hard part is what the assistant must not be able to do. The threat model treats…
articles.body: The problem The request sounds simple: let an AI assistant answer questions from a company's on-premises SQL Server. The hard part is what the assistant must not be able to do. The threat model treats the assistant itself as the attacker: it can be prompt-injected, for example by text stored in a table it just read, or simply make a mistake. The goal is that three things still hold: it cannot change the database, it cannot read outside the connected database, and it cannot get data back from a call before that call is recorded. First, what no gateway fixes: the rows the assistant reads leave the building, to the AI vendor that runs the model. Read-only does not change that. What may be sent, under which personal-data rules (KVKK in Turkey, others elsewhere), is the firm's decision.

articles.title: Freelancer Retainers: Turn One-Off Projects Into Steady Monthly Income
articles.excerpt: Every freelancer knows the feast-and-famine cycle. One month three clients pay at once and the bank account looks generous. The next month the inbox is quiet, the pipeline is empty, and the same bank…
articles.body: Every freelancer knows the feast-and-famine cycle. One month three clients pay at once and the bank account looks generous. The next month the inbox is quiet, the pipeline is empty, and the same bank account starts to feel thin. The work did not get worse. The income just stopped being steady. A retainer fixes the steady part. It is a simple agreement: a client pays a fixed amount every month for a fixed amount of your time, whether they use all of it or not. In the sample, one freelancer replaced the scramble with three retainer clients at $1,300 a month each — $3,900 of income she could count on before the month began — and kept project work on top of it. The retainer did not replace freelancing. It gave freelancing a floor.

articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

articles.excerpt: The California Science Center's brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center —the home of NASA's space shuttle Endeavour —officially opened to the public today (Nov. 13).
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
